read: partial: abstract, introduction, related work, Section 3 (capabilities, difficulty levels, dataset construction, controlled variants), Section 4 (setup, results), conclusion and limitations (pp. 1-9) in full; Appendices A-F.2.2 and G.1-G.5 (pp. 13-27) read; F.3 scoring examples (pp. 20-23) and the subfield figures (p. 28) skimmed
venue_now: Findings of ACL 2026, pp. 36308-36334 (papers.json). The fetched text is arXiv:2509.17677v2, 2 May 2026 (p. 1 footer); it shows no venue header but carries an ACL-style Limitations section and an ACL Code of Ethics statement (pp. 9, 13)
what_it_is: A three-level benchmark of LLM engineering problem solving. Level 1 (single-step formula application) and Level 2 (multi-step, well-defined problems with unique answers) are closed-form problems filtered by an LLM engineering-relevance prompt, with human verification, from existing public benchmarks (SuperGPQA, MMLU, MATH, GSM8K, Orca-Math, HARP, Omni-MATH, Big-Math, competition sets) and university course materials; Level 3 is 43 open-ended modelling problems from CUMCM, MCM/ICM and APMCM (2010-2024) with official rubrics and reference solutions from winning entries (pp. 4-5, 13-15). Each Level 1-2 problem is rewritten by an LLM, with manual verification, into perturbed, knowledge-enhanced and math-abstraction variants; Level 3 gets only a perturbed (paraphrased) variant (pp. 5, 15-17). Levels 1-2 are scored right or wrong against a reference answer by two LLM judges; Level 3 is scored 0-10 per capability (information extraction, domain-specific reasoning, multi-objective decision-making, uncertainty handling) against expert-refined rubrics by the same two LLMs, then calibrated by human annotators (pp. 6, 18-19). Sixteen LLMs are evaluated zero-shot (p. 6).
domain: engineering: three subfields (Systems & Control, Physical & Structural, Chemical & Biological) spanning mechanical, electrical, chemical/biological and other disciplines (pp. 2, 5, 13)
size: 939, 354 and 467 problems in the three subfields (1,760 by my sum; p. 5), of which 43 are Level 3 (p. 5); the text read gives no Level 1/Level 2 split. Three LLM-written variants per Level 1-2 problem, one per Level 3 problem (p. 5). 16 LLMs evaluated (p. 6)
source_of_items: perturbed from existing sets: Levels 1-2 filtered from public benchmarks and competition datasets plus university assignments, exams and teaching content (pp. 5, 13-14); Level 3 collected from modelling competitions (pp. 5, 14-15); variants LLM-generated and manually verified (p. 15)
instances: perturbed: static originals plus fixed LLM-rewritten variants (perturbed, knowledge-enhanced, math abstraction); nothing is regenerated per evaluation (pp. 5, 15-17)
has_gold_traces: partial: Level 3 problems come with official rubrics and reference solutions from top-ranking competition entries (p. 5); Levels 1-2 have reference answers only (released fields, p. 17; scoring, p. 18). The perturbation prompt asks the LLM for a step-by-step 'Rewritten Solution Process' (p. 16), but no solution field is among the released fields listed on p. 17
evaluation: Levels 1-2: final answer, binary, judged by GPT-4.1 and Gemini 2.5 Flash against the reference answer with +/-2% tolerance, disagreements resolved by hand (p. 18). Level 3: rubric scores 0-10 per capability by the same two LLMs, averaged, then reviewed and calibrated by annotators with engineering backgrounds (pp. 6, 19). No step-level or process scoring at any level
human_validation: Level 3 problems and rubrics reviewed by 20 PhD students and engineering professionals (p. 5); each rubric cross-checked by two reviewers with engineering backgrounds, disagreements adjudicated by competition prize-winning experts (p. 19); variants manually verified (p. 15). Level 1-2 judges checked on 300 randomly sampled problems: GPT-4.1 98.67% and Gemini 2.5 Flash 98.33% accurate (p. 18). Level 3: human-calibrated, LLM-only and human-only scores are compared by per-model averages and model ordering (Table 2), with no agreement statistic (pp. 23-24). Human reference score on Level 3: 8.74 (pp. 6-7)
contamination_measures: perturbations: LLM-rewritten variants with numerical and semantic changes 'to assess robustness and reduce possible overlap with pretraining data' (p. 5) and paraphrased Level 3 problems (p. 15). Perturbed accuracy falls from 82.9% to 81.5% on Level 1 and from 66.6% to 61.6% on Level 2 (p. 24); the small Level 3 change (5.372 to 5.341) is read as no sign of contamination (p. 25). The Level 1-2 originals themselves come from public benchmarks (pp. 5, 14)

engtrace_use.sentence: S-E2 (L190-198): 'Others focus on tangential skills such as design generation (Guo et al., 2025b) or software proficiency (Mudur et al., 2025), while broader efforts like EngiBench (Zhou et al., 2025) rely on subjective rubric-based scoring.' S-I3c (L116-122): 'EngTrace addresses both gaps through integrative reasoning templates that, unlike existing benchmarks (e.g., Zhou et al., 2025; Mudur et al., 2025) that rely solely on outcome matching, demand holistic procedural reasoning'. S-E3 (L199-205, closing): 'Evidently, existing benchmarks remain limited to outcome matching and fail to validate the physically grounded reasoning required for engineering.'
engtrace_use.explanation: Each May sentence describes one half of EngiBench, and the two contradict each other (citation map C6). S-E2 (misleading): rubric scoring applies only to the 43 open-ended Level 3 problems (p. 5); Levels 1-2, the great majority of the 939 + 354 + 467 problems (p. 5), are scored right or wrong against a reference answer (pp. 6, 18). 'Subjective' is not supported either: the rubrics are built from official competition scoring standards, finalised by experts, applied by two LLMs and calibrated by people, and LLM-only, calibrated and human-only scores agree closely (pp. 5, 19, 23-24), though no agreement statistic is given. S-I3c (misleading, the protocol's own example): 'rely solely on outcome matching' fits Levels 1-2 (p. 18) but not Level 3, where the content of open-ended solutions is scored by rubric (pp. 6, 19). S-E3 inherits both problems for this paper. What the May text leaves out, and what matters most for EngTrace: EngiBench never checks intermediate results against a reference derivation, its closed-form items are recycled from public math and general benchmarks, and its answer check is an LLM judge, not a deterministic one (pp. 5, 14, 18).

suggested_wording: EngiBench (Zhou et al., 2025) covers three engineering subfields at three levels: its closed-form problems, filtered from existing benchmarks and course materials and rewritten into perturbed, knowledge-enhanced and math-abstraction variants, are scored right or wrong by LLM judges, and its 43 open-ended modelling problems are scored by LLMs against expert-refined competition rubrics; no level checks intermediate results against a reference derivation.
facts_to_cite: Three difficulty levels: foundational knowledge retrieval, contextual reasoning and open-ended modelling (pp. 1, 4).
939, 354 and 467 problems in the Systems & Control, Physical & Structural and Chemical & Biological subfields (p. 5).
Level 1-2 problems are drawn from public benchmarks (SuperGPQA, MMLU, MATH, GSM8K, Orca-Math, HARP, Omni-MATH, Big-Math) and university materials after an engineering-relevance filter (pp. 5, 13-14).
Level 3 has 43 open-ended problems from modelling competitions (CUMCM, MCM/ICM, APMCM, 2010-2024) with official rubrics and reference solutions from top-ranking entries (pp. 5, 14-15).
Each Level 1-2 problem is rewritten into perturbed, knowledge-enhanced and math-abstraction variants by LLM prompting with manual verification; Level 3 has only a perturbed variant (pp. 5, 15).

Levels 1-2 are scored right or wrong against a reference answer by two LLM judges (GPT-4.1, Gemini 2.5 Flash) with +/-2% tolerance; on 300 hand-checked problems the judges were 98.67% and 98.33% accurate (p. 18).
Level 3 is scored 0-10 per capability by the two LLMs against expert-refined rubrics, then calibrated by human annotators (pp. 6, 19).
16 LLMs are evaluated zero-shot (p. 6); accuracy falls under perturbation (Level 2 average 66.6% to 61.6%) and is highest on the math-abstraction variant (pp. 7-8, 24-25).
All models score well below the human reference score of 8.74 on Level 3 (pp. 6-7).
overlap_with_engtrace: Shares: multi-discipline engineering coverage with difficulty tiers (pp. 4-5); a robustness and contamination check by rewritten variants, similar in purpose to EngTrace's paraphrase arm (pp. 5, 24); LLM answer judges spot-checked by hand (p. 18). Lacks: generated instances (static items, most recycled from public benchmarks, pp. 5, 14); gold traces (reference answers only for Levels 1-2, p. 17); step-level evaluation (binary answer or rubric, pp. 18-19); deterministic answer checking (LLM judges at +/-2%, p. 18); expert validation of the evaluator with agreement statistics (a 300-problem accuracy check for Levels 1-2, averages only for Level 3, pp. 18, 23-24). Has what EngTrace lacks: open-ended, under-specified Level 3 tasks and the knowledge-enhanced and math-abstraction diagnostics (pp. 4-5).
notes: Naming clash: Felten et al.'s EngiBench (arXiv:2508.00831) is a different paper, an ML design-optimisation library. Version: the fetched text is v2 of 2 May 2026 (p. 1); the May authors probably read v1 (September 2025), which this review cannot check. The Level 1-2 judge prompt also tells the judge to 'check if the core calculation steps are correct' (p. 18), but it returns only True/False against the reference answer, so this is answer-level scoring, not step evaluation. The first author, Xiyuan Zhou, is also first author of ElecBench (EngiBench reference list, p. 12), which the May paper cites as 'Cheng et al., 2024'. EngiBench's own related work calls FEABench 'task-oriented' evaluation (p. 3).
